Its strings are metal or ox sinew, strung on either side of the case. The frame and supports are also wood. Its plucked attack gives short, clear notes with a firm sense of pitch. The instrument covers the middle to upper middle register, a modest and finely judged span. The resonating case gives the sound a moderate ring, so it is never dry but keeps a soft wooden resonance. The celempung, being larger with longer strings, has a deeper, warmer tone an octave lower and provides the harmonic foundation. Set side by side, the siter is bright and nimble like the dawn light, while the celempung is deep and steady like the earth. In the gamelan the siter's colour falls between the clarity of the pipa and the softness of the harp, with a character of its own.

It is closely related to the kacapi of Sunda, which reflects the exchange and blending of musical cultures between Java and its neighbours. A siter usually has 11 to 13 pairs of strings, tuned to the two traditional Javanese scales, pélog and sléndro. The instrument is finely built, the body about a foot long, and it rests on a wooden case for playing. The celempung developed alongside it as the bass variant, about three feet long and an octave lower. As the gamelan took its place at the centre of the Javanese tradition, the siter became a standard instrument of both court and village performance. Today it survives in traditional Javanese ensembles and has also spread around the world through cultural exchange, becoming an important representative of Southeast Asian music.

The siter is a plucked instrument of the Javanese gamelan in Indonesia, belonging with the kacapi of the Sundanese gamelan to the plucked family. Its box-shaped resonator carries eleven to thirteen pairs of strings on each side, usually tuned to pélog on one side and sléndro on the other; the body is about a foot long and rests on its case when played. The player plucks with the thumbnail and damps with the fingers of both hands, the right hand below the strings and the left above. In the gamelan it is an elaborating instrument, playing melodic patterns over the skeletal melody, at the same speed as the gambang, and it is common in the siter gamelan and other gamelan ensembles.
